title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
description: Brute force to optimized: re-summing every cell per query versus building a 2D prefix sum table once and answering each query with four-term inclusion-exclusion.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a 2D matrix matrix, handle multiple queries of the following type: calculate the sum of the elements of matrix inside the rectangle defined by its upper-left corner (row1, col1) and lower-right corner (row2, col2), inclusive.

blocks.caption: Build a 2D prefix sum table once, then answer every rectangle query in O(1)

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Multiple range queries over a fixed array or matrix","Precompute a prefix sum structure once, then answer each query in O(1) instead of recomputing from scratch"],["The \"range\" is a 2D rectangle, not a 1D interval","A 2D prefix sum table is needed, where each cell holds the sum of the entire rectangle from the origin up to that cell"],["Combining a 2D prefix sum requires more than a simple subtraction","Inclusion-exclusion: add back a corner that gets subtracted twice when removing two overlapping strips"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a 2D matrix matrix, handle multiple queries calculating the sum of elements inside a rectangle defined by an upper-left corner (row1, col1) and a lower-right corner (row2, col2), both inclusive.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Running Total in a Spreadsheet
blocks.text: Like a spreadsheet with a running cumulative total in every cell, letting the sum of any selected rectangular range be read off instantly using its four corner totals, without re-adding every individual cell inside it every time.

blocks.caption: A running cumulative total per cell makes any rectangle's sum instantly readable

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Each query's rectangle can be anywhere in the matrix and any size, yet every one of them should be answered without re-scanning the matrix from scratch.
Edge case: a single-cell query
When row1 equals row2 and col1 equals col2, the "rectangle" is really just one cell, and the technique should still return exactly that cell's value.
5. How Should We Think?

Before summing each rectangle directly, notice that many overlapping rectangle queries share most of their cells, and a 1D-style prefix sum idea, extended to two dimensions, can turn every query into a handful of lookups.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The same idea as a 1D prefix sum applies here: precompute cumulative sums once so any range's sum becomes a difference of a few precomputed values, avoiding repeated re-summation.

Observation 2: In 2D, define prefix[i][j] as the sum of the entire rectangle from the matrix's top-left corner (0,0) up to, but not including, row i and column j. Every cell's prefix value already bundles every row and column before it.

Observation 3: Building this table incrementally works because each cell's prefix value equals its own matrix value, plus the prefix total directly above it, plus the prefix total directly to its left, minus the prefix total diagonally up-left, which removes the region counted by both the above and left additions.

Observation 4: Answering a query for rectangle (row1,col1) to (row2,col2) needs the same inclusion-exclusion idea in reverse: take the full top-left rectangle down to (row2,col2), subtract the strip above row1, subtract the strip left of col1, then add back the small corner rectangle that got subtracted twice, once in each strip.

Whenever a range-sum query needs to work over a 2D grid instead of a 1D array, build a 2D prefix sum table the same way as 1D, but combine any four corner values using inclusion-exclusion, add, subtract, subtract, add back, instead of a single subtraction.

This "add the top-left rectangle, subtract two overshooting strips, add back the double-removed corner" pattern is the standard way any 2D range-sum or range-count problem is solved once a cumulative table has been built.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each query, directly walk every cell inside the requested rectangle and add it to a running total.
Step by step algorithm

items: Store the matrix as-is when the object is constructed, doing no precomputation.
For every query, loop over every row from row1 to row2 and every column from col1 to col2, summing each cell directly.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The constructor does no work beyond storing a reference to the matrix, since brute force intentionally defers all computation to query time.
The nested loops are bounded exactly by the query's own rectangle, never touching cells outside it.
A fresh running total starts at zero for every single query, since no work is reused between queries.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every query directly re-sums exactly the cells it needs, so the correct rectangle sum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) construction; each query is O(rows times cols) in the worst case.
Space: O(1) extra beyond storing the matrix reference.

Limitation: revisiting every cell inside a rectangle for every single query wastes enormous repeated work when the same matrix is queried many times, since the vast majority of the addition being done during one query is identical to work already done during a previous, overlapping query.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force redoes the same additions again and again across overlapping queries, since two nearby rectangles share almost all of their cells. A 2D prefix sum table fixes exactly this: build it once, in O(rows times cols) time, so every cell's cumulative top-left-rectangle-sum is available instantly, and then every future query, no matter how many there are, needs only four lookups and three arithmetic operations, regardless of how large the requested rectangle is.

Precompute a prefix sum table one row and one column larger than the matrix, where prefix[i][j] holds the sum of every cell strictly above row i and strictly left of column j. Build it incrementally using each cell's own value plus the prefix total above it plus the prefix total to its left, minus the doubly-counted corner. Then answer sumRegion(row1,col1,row2,col2) using the four-corner inclusion-exclusion formula.
9. Optimized Solution
Build a 2D prefix sum table once, then answer every query with a single four-term formula.
Dry run: building the prefix table for a smaller 3x3 example
For clarity, here is the build process traced on a smaller 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]; the exact same steps apply to the full-size matrix above.

blocks.text: Dry run: answering sumRegion(1, 1, 2, 2) on the same 3x3 example
This rectangle covers rows 1-2 and columns 1-2, meaning the cells 5, 6, 8, 9, whose direct sum is 28.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Term","Value","Why"],"rows":[["prefix[row2+1][col2+1] = prefix[3][3]","45","The full top-left rectangle down to the bottom-right corner of the query"],["- prefix[row1][col2+1] = - prefix[1][3]","-6","Removes the strip of rows above row1, row 0 only, values 1+2+3=6"],["- prefix[row2+1][col1] = - prefix[3][1]","-12","Removes the strip of columns left of col1, column 0 only, values 1+4+7=12"],["+ prefix[row1][col1] = + prefix[1][1]","+1","Adds back the top-left corner cell, value 1, which both strips above removed once each, so it must be restored"],["Total","45 - 6 - 12 + 1 = 28","Matches the direct sum of 5+6+8+9=28"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols) construction; O(1) per query.
Space: O(rows times cols), for the prefix sum table.
Why This Works

Each prefix[i][j] cell holds the sum of the entire rectangle from the matrix's origin to (i-1, j-1), so subtracting the strip above the query and the strip left of the query removes everything outside the requested rectangle in two passes, one for rows and one for columns. But the small rectangle in the very top-left corner, shared by both of those removed strips, gets subtracted twice as a result, once in each strip's removal, so it must be added back exactly once to correct the total. This add-subtract-subtract-add pattern is inclusion-exclusion applied to areas instead of sets.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Term","Role"],"rows":[["prefix[row2+1][col2+1]","Everything from the origin down to the query's bottom-right corner, an over-count that includes far more than just the requested rectangle"],["- prefix[row1][col2+1]","Removes everything above the query's top edge, but only within the query's own columns and everything left of them"],["- prefix[row2+1][col1]","Removes everything left of the query's left edge, but only within the query's own rows and everything above them"],["+ prefix[row1][col1]","Restores the shared top-left corner rectangle that both removals above subtracted, correcting the double removal"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The prefix table is built with one extra row and one extra column of zeros along the top and left edges, so every real cell's formula can safely reference "prefix above" and "prefix left" without any special-casing for row 0 or column 0.
Each prefix cell is computed in a single pass using only already-computed neighbors, above, left, and diagonal, so the entire table is built in one O(rows times cols) sweep.
Every query uses the same four-term formula regardless of the rectangle's size or position, which is exactly what makes each query O(1).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

A 2D prefix sum table is the direct generalization of a 1D prefix sum array: each cell aggregates an entire rectangle instead of a single interval, and combining four such values needs inclusion-exclusion instead of a simple two-term subtraction.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the extra padding row and column of zeros, which forces awkward special-casing for queries touching row 0 or column 0 instead of a single uniform formula.
Using only two terms, like the 1D case, instead of the full four-term inclusion-exclusion formula, which silently double-subtracts the shared top-left corner.
Mixing up whether prefix[i][j] includes row i and column j themselves or stops just before them, which shifts every index in the formula by one and produces subtly wrong sums.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Draw the four-rectangle picture, or describe it out loud, before writing the formula, since inclusion-exclusion is much easier to get right visually than purely algebraically.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Answer many range-sum queries efficiently over a fixed 2D matrix" points toward building a 2D prefix sum table once in O(rows times cols), then answering every query in O(1) using the four-term inclusion-exclusion formula.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: What if the matrix could be updated between queries? A flat prefix sum table no longer works efficiently, since a single update would require rebuilding a whole row or column; a 2D Binary Indexed Tree, or a segment tree, would be needed instead, trading O(1) queries for O(log rows times log cols) updates and queries.

How would you extend this to a 3D grid? The same inclusion-exclusion idea generalizes, but combining a corner now needs eight terms instead of four, alternating sign based on how many of the three dimensions each term overshoots.

How is this related to the 1D Range Sum Query - Immutable problem? It is the exact same idea one dimension higher: a 1D prefix sum needs a two-term subtraction, while a 2D prefix sum needs a four-term inclusion-exclusion, and a 3D version would need eight terms.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Direct 2D generalization of Range Sum Query - Immutable, replacing a single subtraction with four-term inclusion-exclusion.
Same "precompute once, answer every query in O(1)" philosophy as every other immutable prefix sum problem in this category.
Same inclusion-exclusion structure reused in problems like Matrix Block Sum, which layers a sliding query rectangle on top of this exact same 2D prefix sum table.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) construction, O(rows times cols) per query.
Optimized (2D prefix sum table): O(rows times cols) construction, O(1) per query.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Build a 2D prefix sum table once, then answer every rectangle-sum query in O(1) using four-term inclusion-exclusion
Core Idea: Each prefix[i][j] holds the sum of the entire top-left rectangle ending at (i-1,j-1); combining four such values with add-subtract-subtract-add isolates exactly the requested rectangle
Time: O(rows times cols) construction, O(1) per query
Space: O(rows times cols)
Most Important Observation: A 2D range-sum query is answered the same way as a 1D one, generalized from a two-term subtraction to a four-term inclusion-exclusion formula
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Big rectangle, minus top strip, minus left strip, plus back the corner counted twice
